questions.prompt: Why are quantity edits stored as keyed overrides instead of mutating the recipe data, and why do they stay free-form strings?

keyPoints.text: The recipes are reference data while the shopping list is the user's own state.
keyPoints.quote: The cookbook is reference data; the shopping list is user state.

keyPoints.text: Mutating a recipe's ingredient array would leak user edits into the recipe-detail screen.
keyPoints.quote: could change the recipe-detail screen unintentionally

keyPoints.text: An override map is the smaller change and keeps the source untouched.
keyPoints.quote: A keyed override is smaller and preserves the source.

keyPoints.text: Quantities are not parsed or scaled because the text is richer than a number.
keyPoints.quote: values can contain fractions, ranges, package sizes

keyPoints.text: The fallback uses nullish coalescing so a deliberately cleared quantity stays cleared.
The fallback lives in ingredientsWithQuantities, which feeds both the screen and the clipboard.

questions.prompt: What is an invariant in this project's sense, and how do you turn one into something testable?

keyPoints.text: An invariant is a rule that holds both before and after an operation runs.
keyPoints.quote: must remain true before and after an operation

keyPoints.text: A claim like the app working as a whole cannot be tested directly.
The project's behavior statement supplies concrete invariants, such as cleanup on removal.
Each sentence becomes a small state table with fixed columns.
keyPoints.quote: initial state, input, expected final state and expected feedback

keyPoints.text: The table should cover at least one rejection and one repeated action.
keyPoints.quote: one rejected input and one retry/repeated action

keyPoints.text: A good invariant outlives the implementation it currently describes.
keyPoints.quote: even if the implementation changes from an array to a database

questions.prompt: Distinguish validation from normalization at this app's storage boundary, and explain how the same job would look on a server.

keyPoints.text: Validation refuses input the operation cannot accept.
keyPoints.quote: Validation rejects values the operation cannot accept.

keyPoints.text: Normalization reshapes acceptable input into the expected representation.
keyPoints.quote: converts acceptable values to the representation the rest of the program expects

keyPoints.text: Neither step may fabricate data that was not there.
keyPoints.quote: Neither operation should silently invent facts.

keyPoints.text: Anything that crossed a boundary deserves the unknown type, not trust.
keyPoints.quote: is the honest type for anything that crossed a boundary

keyPoints.text: JSON.parse hands back any, which quietly turns the compiler off.
keyPoints.quote: it silently disables the checks you think you have

keyPoints.text: Every boundary needs the same four steps the normalizer performs.
keyPoints.quote: shape guard, type check, domain check, bound

keyPoints.text: The failure policy differs by boundary: the browser drops bad keys quietly, an API answers with a 400.
keyPoints.quote: the browser silently drops the bad key because there is no one to tell
